initial.text:
‹ EXPERIENCE
GENERATIVE MOLECULAR MODELING

GENERATIVE MOLECULAR MODELING  /  EXPERIENCE · 2025

Molecules need representation before generation.

During an AI/ML research internship in generative molecular modeling, I learned how molecular structures become SMILES and model-ready features before exploring generation.

RESEARCH ROLE

AI / ML Research Intern
Generative Molecular Modeling

PERIOD

March – June 2025
Computational chemistry · Biomedical research

01 / MODEL REPRESENTATION

Represent the molecule first.

I moved from molecular structures to SMILES, then used RDKit to parse and validate the representation.
April 12 snapshot: 15,696 rows · 14,487 unique SMILES.
Curated experimental subsets: ~400–600 entries.

SCHEMATIC · NOT A PROJECT SAMPLE
Representation path: a molecular structure is encoded as a SMILES string, then a Morgan fingerprint with radius 2 and 128 bits.

STRUCTURE

→
SMILES
string format
→

MORGAN FINGERPRINT

radius 2 · 128 bits
Illustrative bit marks

02 / EXPERIMENT ROUTES

Three approaches. Different outcomes.

I explored sequence generation, fragment-based design, and another generative workflow.

01 / SEQUENCE GENERATION

DeepMol
CSVLoader
→
SMILES sequences
→
RNN MolecularGenerator

Why: generate from molecules represented as SMILES sequences. Input: curated experimental SMILES loaded through DeepMol CSVLoader. Method: RNN MolecularGenerator.

METHOD

Recorded RNN run settings: 10 epochs; batch size 64.
My work covered data loading, SMILES processing, and sequence-generation work. Learning: molecular representation shaped this route.

02 / FRAGMENT-BASED DESIGN

RDKit + Fragmenstein
Structure
→
Fragment selection
→
Recombination

Why: explore structure-based design alongside sequence generation. Input: molecular structures and compatible fragments. Method: select, link, and recombine with RDKit / Fragmenstein.

OUTCOME

Some fragment workflows succeeded
My work covered fragment selection, linking, and spatial workflows with RDKit / Fragmenstein. Learning: this route depends on structural fit and spatial context.

03 / ATTEMPTED GENERATION

REINVENT4
REINVENT4 researched
→
Generation attempted

Generation attempt did not succeed.

OUTCOME

No successful generation
Why: test another generative approach alongside sequence and fragment work. I researched REINVENT4 and attempted generation. The available notes do not record its input, configuration, or why generation did not succeed. Learning: this remained an exploratory attempt, not a demonstrated generation workflow.

03 / PROJECT OUTPUT

A project output in SMILES.

PROJECT OUTPUT · DEEPMOL

500
generated SMILES samples

04 / MY CONTRIBUTION

Research engineering across the workflow.

My DeepMol contribution covered data loading, SMILES processing, molecular features and sequence generation; I also worked on fragment workflows.

TECHNICAL LEARNING

Sequence vs. fragments

DeepMol's SMILES sequence path differed from fragment selection and recombination; comparing the two made molecular representation a core modeling choice.

WHAT I CARRIED FORWARD

I left with a habit of making each workflow clear and stating what each experiment actually showed.

LIVING IN SILICO  /  GENERATIVE MOLECULAR MODELING

initial.text:
CREST

EXPENSE INTELLIGENCE / REVIEW WORKFLOW

Crest

Crest is an expense intelligence workspace for reviewing requests with budget, spend history and policy context.

It helps finance teams spot unusual patterns and prepare requests for preapproval; a person reviews the context and decides what happens next.

SAMPLE DATA
Expense review / policy context / preapproval
WATCH DEMO ↗
One transaction. Two sources. Human review.

Transactions move through deterministic finance and policy checks. Rule-based signals and retrieved policy context support review; people retain decision authority.

A sample expense branches into deterministic budget and spend checks and retrieved policy context interpreted by Gemini; both inform human review.
01 REQUEST
02 TWO EVIDENCE PATHS
03 HUMAN DECISION

Conference registration
$1,200
TRAVEL & EVENTS
DETERMINISTIC SIGNALS
Budget + spend rules

Budget · prior spend · thresholds

RETRIEVED POLICY
Relevant passages

Matched to the request

POLICY INTERPRETATION
Gemini

Reads retrieved policy context

DECISION AUTHORITY
HUMAN REVIEW

A reviewer weighs the context and chooses the next action.

APPROVE
DENY
FINANCE Q&A + REPORTING
FINANCE QUESTION
→
FINANCE Q&A ANSWER
REPORTING NEED
→
REPORT VIEW

Finance questions → transaction-backed answers; reporting needs → report views. Separate from the standalone policy-PDF retrieval prototype.

DECISION SYSTEM / GROUNDED POLICY, DETERMINISTIC AUTHORITY
Policy context. Deterministic decisions.

A standalone prototype indexed a Brim policy PDF and retrieved passages for Gemini; a live endpoint or deployed workflow was not verified. Finance and policy rules remained authoritative; anomaly heuristics surfaced review cues.

RETRIEVED POLICY CONTEXT
Gemini interpreted the top retrieved passages.

Grounded context supported review; it did not detect or decide.

+
DETERMINISTIC RULES + SIGNALS
Finance and policy rules remained authoritative.

Heuristic split cue: group by employee, merchant, day. Each charge is below threshold; combined total reaches it. Review only.

→
HUMAN REVIEW
Sample queue uses budget + employee history.

Gemini recommendation or template fallback; human approve/deny is recorded locally in the prototype.

TECHNICAL OWNERSHIP

I built backend workflows for human review.

I built Policy Compliance Engine workflows, deterministic anomaly signals, policy retrieval, and part of preapproval.

WORK I BUILT

POLICY ENGINE
Compliance workflows
ANOMALY SIGNALS
Deterministic rules
POLICY RETRIEVAL
Relevant passages
PREAPPROVAL
Part of the workflow
3RD PLACE
BRIM FINANCIAL CHALLENGE · MPC HACKS 2026
PROJECT RECORD ↗

ENGINEERING PRINCIPLE

Signals organize review. People own the decision.

The challenge presentation ran over its allotted time. I learned to explain the decision path concisely: rules, policy context, then human review.
